sections.skill: Explain how bonds work and calculate bond interest

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: What does an investor do when buying a bond?

choices.text: Lends money to the issuer in return for interest and repayment
Buys ownership in the issuer and a vote at shareholder meetings
Opens an insured deposit at a bank branch
Pays a fee for the right to buy stock later

questions.correct_answer: Lends money to the issuer in return for interest and repayment
questions.intro: A bond is a loan from the investor to an issuer, such as a company, a city, or the U.S. government. The issuer promises to pay interest (the coupon) on a schedule and repay the face value at maturity. Bonds are investments, not deposits, and can lose value.
questions.feedback: Bondholders are lenders; stockholders are owners.
questions.topic: Bonds: lending to governments and companies

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A $1,000 bond has a 4% coupon rate. How much interest does it pay per year?
questions.intro: Yearly coupon interest = face value × coupon rate. Many bonds pay half of it every six months.
questions.topic: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
sources: SEC Investor.gov: When interest rates rise, prices of existing bonds generally fall; bonds carry interest rate risk and credit (default) risk. (https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/bonds-or-fixed-income-products/bonds)

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Ivy owns a bond paying 3%. New bonds now pay 5%. What usually happens to the market price of Ivy's bond?

choices.text: It rises
It falls
It stays exactly at face value no matter what
It turns into a 5% bond automatically

questions.intro: Existing bond prices move opposite to interest rates. When rates rise, older bonds paying lower coupons become less attractive, so their prices fall; when rates fall, their prices rise. This is interest rate risk.
questions.feedback: Rising rates lower the price of existing lower-coupon bonds.
questions.topic: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
sources: SEC Investor.gov: When interest rates rise, prices of existing bonds generally fall; bonds carry interest rate risk and credit (default) risk. (https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/bonds-or-fixed-income-products/bonds)

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which bond generally has the LOWEST risk of default?

choices.text: A bond from a new company with heavy debt
A "junk" bond with a low credit rating
A U.S. Treasury bond
A bond from a company that recently missed payments

questions.intro: Credit (default) risk is the chance the issuer cannot pay. Ratings agencies grade bonds; "investment grade" bonds have lower risk, and "high-yield" ("junk") bonds have higher risk and higher interest. U.S. Treasury securities are backed by the U.S. government.
questions.feedback: Treasuries are backed by the U.S. government and have very low default risk.
questions.topic: Bonds: lending to governments and companies

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A $1,000 bond paying $50 a year is bought for $950. What is its current yield (nearest tenth of a percent)?
questions.intro: Current yield = yearly interest ÷ current price × 100. Buying below face value raises the yield.
questions.topic: Bonds: lending to governments and companies

misconceptions.D: Gives the price as a percent

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Interest from many municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax. Why might a high-income investor prefer one paying 3% over a taxable bond paying 4%?

choices.text: After tax, the municipal bond may keep more income
Municipal bonds can never lose value
Taxable bonds always default
The 3% bond pays more before tax, so it always wins

questions.correct_answer: After tax, the municipal bond may keep more income
questions.intro: Municipal bonds are issued by states and cities. Their interest is often exempt from federal income tax, so their after-tax yield can beat a higher taxable yield.
questions.feedback: Tax-exempt interest can be worth more after tax.
questions.topic: Bonds: lending to governments and companies

questions.prompt: An investor in the 32% federal tax bracket gets 4% from a taxable bond. What is the after-tax yield?
questions.intro: After-tax yield = taxable yield × (1 − tax rate).

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which statement about U.S. Treasury bills, notes, and bonds is TRUE?

choices.text: They are issued by private companies, not the government
They are FDIC insured deposits
They differ mainly by how long until they mature
They pay no interest of any kind

questions.correct_answer: They differ mainly by how long until they mature
questions.intro: Treasury bills mature in a year or less, notes in 2 to 10 years, and bonds in 20 or 30 years.
questions.feedback: Bills, notes, and bonds are Treasury securities of different lengths.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A high-yield ("junk") bond pays 8%, while an investment-grade bond pays 5%. Why the difference?

choices.text: The high-yield issuer is more likely to default
High-yield bonds are insured by the federal government
Investment-grade bonds have longer maturities, always
The difference is random

questions.correct_answer: The high-yield issuer is more likely to default
questions.intro: Riskier borrowers must pay higher interest to attract lenders.
questions.feedback: Higher yield compensates for higher default risk.
questions.topic: Bonds: lending to governments and companies

misconceptions.B: Believes higher yield comes with a guarantee
misconceptions.C: Attributes the gap only to maturity
misconceptions.D: Misses the link between risk and yield

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A bond fund holds bonds from hundreds of different companies and governments. What is one advantage over buying one bond?

choices.text: It can never lose value
It always pays the same fixed income each year
It is FDIC insured
Default risk is spread across many issuers

questions.correct_answer: Default risk is spread across many issuers
questions.intro: Bond funds pool money to buy many bonds. Owning many issuers spreads credit risk (a fund of hundreds of Treasuries, by contrast, has one issuer). Fund prices still change with interest rates.
questions.feedback: Owning many issuers spreads credit risk, though fund prices still move with rates.

questions.intro: At maturity, a bond repays its face value, no matter what it was bought for. The last interest payment is usually paid at the same time, separately from the principal.
questions.feedback: At maturity the issuer repays the full $1,000 face value as principal.

questions.prompt: Bought at $900 and repaid at $1,000 at maturity, what is the gain on price alone?
questions.intro: Gain on price = amount received at maturity − price paid.
questions.feedback: $1,000 − $900 = $100, plus coupon interest along the way.
